opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core of it is that people are usually pretty bad at writing a complete prompt up front, and that's not a knock on users; it's just how people communicate. When you ask a colleague to go research something, you'd have a quick conversation first: "What's this for? How deep do you want me to go? Do you care about recent stuff or the whole history? Should I focus on any particular angle?" A good research assistant asks those questions before disappearing for a few hours.

With Deep Research the stakes are higher than in a normal chat, because the model goes off and works for five, ten, twenty minutes, reading dozens or hundreds of sources. If it starts from a misunderstanding of what you wanted, you don't find out until the end, and then you've wasted all that time and compute. With a regular chat model, if the first answer is off, you just correct it and get a new answer a few seconds later. Here the feedback loop is much slower, so it's worth spending a little effort up front to get the intent right.

There's also something subtle. Often the user doesn't fully know what they want until they're asked. The clarifying question makes you think, "Actually, I care more about the comparison between these two options than a general overview," or "I'm looking at this for an investment decision, not just curiosity." That context changes which sources the model prioritizes, how it structures the report, and what it treats as important. So that short back and forth is cheap, but it pays off a lot in how relevant and useful the final output is.

r002.rationale: It explains that clarifying questions help users specify their purpose, desired depth, timeframe, and focus, making the research request more detailed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way to put it is that the clarifying questions are there to close the gap between what you typed and what you actually want. Most research questions, if you look at them honestly, are massively underspecified. If I say "give me an overview of the state of the art in protein structure prediction," there are a dozen reasonable interpretations of that. Do I care about the last six months or the last ten years? Am I an expert who wants the details on the architectures, or am I a product person who wants to know what's commercially usable? Do I want papers, or do I want companies?

A human research assistant would never just run off and spend five hours on that. They'd ask you two or three questions first, because they know that the cost of guessing wrong is really high when the task is long. And that's the key thing with Deep Research: the model is about to go spend a lot of compute, read a lot of sources, and produce something long. If it's pointed in slightly the wrong direction at the start, that error compounds across the whole trajectory. You end up with a beautifully formatted report on the wrong question.

So the back and forth is really about front-loading the cheapest possible intervention. A few seconds of your time clarifying intent saves a ton of wasted work downstream, and it also makes the final output much more satisfying because it's actually scoped to what you cared about rather than to the model's best guess.

The other thing I'd say is that it changes the user's relationship to the output. When you've answered those questions, you've sort of co-authored the plan, so when the report comes back you already know what it's going to cover and why. That makes it a lot easier to trust and to act on, versus getting a wall of text and having to reverse-engineer what assumptions the model made.

r001.rationale: The response explains that clarification captures the user's intended scope and preferences, so the research follows what they actually care about rather than the model's guess.

r002.rationale: It says the back-and-forth closes the gap between the typed question and the user's intent, resolving underspecification and helping define the research plan.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps because the initial prompt usually leaves a lot unsaid. You have some context in your head about what you’re trying to accomplish, what you already know, and what would make the answer useful. The model doesn’t necessarily have that context.

So that initial back and forth is a way to get aligned on the task before it goes off and spends a lot of time researching. Are you looking for a broad overview, or are you trying to make a specific decision? What constraints matter? Those answers can change which questions it investigates and what evidence it looks for.

And sometimes you haven’t fully worked that out yourself. Having the model ask a good question helps you clarify what you actually want. So you end up with a better research task, which gives you a much better chance of getting a useful result.

r001.rationale: The response says the exchange aligns the task and can change what the model investigates, but does not state that Deep Research closely follows nuances in the initial question’s framing.

r002.rationale: It explains that clarifying goals, constraints, and useful evidence helps shape a better research task, improving the chance of a useful result.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to figuring out what you actually want. When you ask a research question, there’s usually a bunch of context in your head that doesn’t make it into the prompt. What are you going to use the answer for? How deep do you want to go? What constraints matter?

That initial back and forth gives the system a chance to surface those things before it goes off and does a lot of work. Otherwise, it can do a very thorough job of answering a slightly different question. And it helps you clarify your own thinking, too. Sometimes you don’t know exactly what you’re looking for until somebody asks you a good follow-up question.

r001.rationale: The response says clarification prevents Deep Research from answering a slightly different question, but does not clearly state that it closely follows nuances in the initial question’s framing.

r002.rationale: It explains that the back-and-forth surfaces intended use, desired depth, and constraints, helping the user make the research request more specific.
